narrative:
The model determined that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the average of students who were admitted, giving the model some confidence in your academic foundation.

However, your class rank in the third year of law school pulled strongly in the opposite direction. Placing in the second decile (compared to an average around the sixth decile for admitted students) signaled to the model that you may struggle to keep pace with your peers, increasing the predicted risk of bar exam failure. This was the second most important factor.

Your family income bracket ranked third. Being in the lower-middle income group slightly raised the chance of failure relative to most admitted students, who are overwhelmingly from upper-middle or middle brackets.

Taken together, the model saw your solid undergraduate record outweighed by weaker performance once you reached law school and by socioeconomic factors that can affect support systems and study resources.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the remaining law school years, seek out academic support or tutoring early, and consider part-time work that leaves more study time. Strengthening your upper-level performance is the clearest way to shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
